analysis.one_liner: Extends emergency unemployment benefits by 13 extra weeks, paid for by trimming the business meal-and-entertainment tax deduction.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by Rep. Chester Atkins with 46 Democratic cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: During the recession of the early 1990s, this bill would have extended emergency unemployment checks for an additional 13 weeks and restored earlier benefit reductions. To pay for it, the bill would have trimmed the federal tax deduction businesses take for meals and entertainment from 80% of the cost to 70%. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Long-term unemployed workers who had exhausted their regular state benefits, who would have received up to 13 more weeks of emergency payments; some workers whose payments had been reduced under the 1991 emergency program would have had those amounts restored.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Emergency Unemployment Compensation Act of 1991 to add 13 weeks to the limit on emergency unemployment payments.
It also waives, for weeks paid before June 13, 1992, a reduction in the amount payable, and raises the applicable benefit percentage by 50 percentage points.
The cost is offset by reducing the business tax deduction for meals and entertainment expenses from 80 percent to 70 percent of the expense.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that claim the meal and entertainment deduction — primarily employers that expense client dinners, entertainment, and similar costs — would bear the cost through a smaller tax write-off (70% instead of 80%).
analysis.who_pays_short: Businesses deducting meal and entertainment costs

drawbacks.text: The offset is a tax increase on businesses during a recession; restaurants, hotels, and entertainment venues argued such deduction cuts reduce expense-account business, and defenders of the 80% deduction say it supports hospitality and tourism employment.
The extra 13 weeks are temporary emergency aid that expires with the program rather than a structural fix, so workers could face the same cliff again once the extension ran out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a jobless worker whose benefits had run out, 13 more weeks of income during a deep recession is worth far more than the cost of a smaller deduction on business dinners, which falls on companies rather than individuals. The main honest objection is that taxing business entertainment in a weak economy adds a small drag at a bad time, but the direct relief to unemployed households is the larger effect.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Human Resources Subcommittee the day it was introduced, and it sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Chester Atkins introduced the bill on July 23, 1992, joined by 13 original cosponsors including other members of the Massachusetts delegation.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means and then to that committee's Subcommittee on Human Resources.
The bill would have added 13 weeks to emergency unemployment compensation and reversed payment reductions for weeks paid before mid-June 1992.
It would have paid for the extension by cutting the business meal and entertainment deduction from 80 percent to 70 percent.
The bill attracted 46 Democratic cosponsors, all in the House, but the record shows no further committee or floor action after the initial referral.
Congress adjourned on January 3, 1993, ending the bill's chances; it never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that claim the 80% meal and entertainment deduction kept the more generous write-off, and no cost was imposed on the hospitality industry. Unemployed workers did not benefit from this particular bill, though Congress did pass separate unemployment extension legislation later in 1992 by other means.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Businesses keeping the larger tax write-off

for.name: Chester G. Atkins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 13 original cosponsors from both parties' benches (all Democrats) on the day of introduction.

for.name: 46 of 267 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it visible bipartisan-delegation backing within the House Democratic caucus.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred never reported it out; no markup or hearing on H.R. 5681 is recorded, and the bill died in the Human Resources Subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship was Democratic — the sponsor and 46 Democratic cosponsors — but no vote was ever taken in committee or on the floor, so the partisan shape of any actual opposition was never tested.

industries.note: The bill's funding offset trims the business meal and entertainment deduction from 80% to 70%, raising the after-tax cost of expense-account meals and events and likely reducing some of this business. The industry's interest in keeping the larger deduction ran directly against the unemployed workers the bill aimed to help.
Any business that deducts client meals or entertainment would pay somewhat more in taxes under the offset. The cost is modest per firm but is the explicit price of the unemployment extension.
